scenes.text: There's a frog that freezes almost solid every winter, then comes back to life in spring.
It's the wood frog, and it lives in the northern forests of Alaska and Canada.
In autumn it just hides in leaf litter on the forest floor.
As the temperature drops, ice forms in its belly, around its organs, and between its skin and muscle.
It stops breathing, and no muscle moves at all.
To survive, its liver floods every cell with huge amounts of sugar.
That sugar works like antifreeze, stopping ice from forming inside its cells.
Scientists studying frogs in Alaska found up to sixty percent of the body can turn to ice.
Before winter really sets in, they can freeze and thaw ten to fifteen times.
Then they stay frozen for as long as seven months.
When spring finally warms the ground, the frog thaws from the inside out.
First the heart starts beating again, then the brain switches on, and finally the legs move.
Scientists still don't fully understand what restarts its heart.
Would you rather freeze through the winter or stay awake for all of it? Comment below.

title: This frog freezes solid and comes back to life 🧊
caption: Wood frogs in Alaska stop breathing and their hearts stop for months in winter. Sugar acts as antifreeze inside their cells, and in spring they thaw from the inside out.
